For parabola $y^2=4ax$, the slope of chord joining parameter points $t_1$ and $t_2$ is

$$ \frac{2a(t_2-t_1)}{a(t_2^2-t_1^2)}=\frac{2}{t_1+t_2}. $$

So slope of chord joining parameter $1$ and $t_1$ is

$$ m_{BA}=\frac{2}{1+t_1}, $$

and slope of chord joining parameter $1$ and $t_2$ is

$$ m_{BC}=\frac{2}{1+t_2}. $$

Since these are perpendicular,

$$ \frac{2}{1+t_1}\cdot \frac{2}{1+t_2}=-1. $$

Hence

$$ \frac{4}{(1+t_1)(1+t_2)}=-1 $$

which gives

$$ (1+t_1)(1+t_2)=-4. $$

So,

$$ t_1t_2+t_1+t_2+1=-4 $$

or

$$ t_1t_2+t_1+t_2=-5. $$

Now let the centroid of $\triangle ABC$ be $G(h,k)$.

Using centroid formula,

$$ h=\frac{4t_1^2+4+4t_2^2}{3} =\frac{4}{3}(t_1^2+t_2^2+1), $$

$$ k=\frac{8t_1+8+8t_2}{3} =\frac{8}{3}(t_1+t_2+1). $$

Let

$$ S=t_1+t_2, \qquad P=t_1t_2. $$

Then from the perpendicularity condition,

$$ P+S=-5. $$

Also,

$$ t_1^2+t_2^2=S^2-2P. $$

So

$$ h=\frac{4}{3}(S^2-2P+1). $$

Since $P=-5-S$,

$$ h=\frac{4}{3}\bigl(S^2-2(-5-S)+1\bigr) $$

$$ h=\frac{4}{3}(S^2+2S+11). $$

Also,

$$ k=\frac{8}{3}(S+1). $$

From this,

$$ S+1=\frac{3k}{8} \quad \Rightarrow \quad S=\frac{3k}{8}-1. $$

Substitute into $h$:

$$ h=\frac{4}{3}\left[\left(\frac{3k}{8}-1\right)^2+2\left(\frac{3k}{8}-1\right)+11\right]. $$

Now simplify:

$$ \left(\frac{3k}{8}-1\right)^2=\frac{9k^2}{64}-\frac{3k}{4}+1 $$

and

$$ 2\left(\frac{3k}{8}-1\right)=\frac{3k}{4}-2. $$

So inside the bracket,

$$ \frac{9k^2}{64}-\frac{3k}{4}+1+\frac{3k}{4}-2+11 = \frac{9k^2}{64}+10. $$

Hence

$$ h=\frac{4}{3}\left(\frac{9k^2}{64}+10\right) =\frac{3k^2}{16}+\frac{40}{3}. $$

Therefore,

$$ h-\frac{40}{3}=\frac{3k^2}{16}. $$

Rearranging,

$$ k^2=\frac{16}{3}\left(h-\frac{40}{3}\right). $$

So the locus is a parabola:

$$ k^2=4a\left(h-\frac{40}{3}\right) $$

with

$$ 4a=\frac{16}{3} \quad \Rightarrow \quad a=\frac{4}{3}. $$

Length of latus rectum of this parabola is

$$ 4a=\frac{16}{3}. $$

Therefore, three times the length of latus rectum is

$$ 3\times \frac{16}{3}=16. $$

So the required answer is

$$ \boxed{16}. $$

subject: mathematics
question_text: Let $$f$$ be twice differentiable function such that $$f(x) = \displaystyle\int_0^x \tan(t - x)\,dt - \int_0^x f(t)\tan t\,dt$$, $$x \in \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$. Then $$f''\!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) + 12f'\!\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) + f\!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$$ is equal to :

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
We are given
$$f(x)=\int_{0}^{x}\tan(t-x)\,dt-\int_{0}^{x}f(t)\tan t\,dt,\qquad x\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right).$$

Step 1: Evaluate the first integral.
Put $$s=t-x.$$ When $$t=0,\;s=-x$$ and when $$t=x,\;s=0.$$ Thus $$\int_{0}^{x}\tan(t-x)\,dt=\int_{-x}^{0}\tan s\,ds.$$ Since $$\int\tan s\,ds=-\ln|\cos s|,$$ we get $$\int_{-x}^{0}\tan s\,ds=\Big[-\ln|\cos s|\Big]_{-x}^{0}=0+\ln\cos x=\ln\cos x.$$

Therefore $$f(x)=\ln\cos x-\int_{0}^{x}f(t)\tan t\,dt.\qquad -(1)$$

Step 2: Differentiate once.
Differentiate both sides of $$(1)$$ with respect to $$x$$ (using Leibniz rule for the integral): $$f'(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(\ln\cos x\bigr)-f(x)\tan x.$$ Because $$\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\cos x=-\tan x,$$ we get $$f'(x)=-\tan x-f(x)\tan x=-\tan x\bigl(1+f(x)\bigr).\qquad -(2)$$

Step 3: Differentiate again.
Differentiate $$(2):$$ $$f''(x)=-\sec^{2}x\bigl(1+f(x)\bigr)-\tan x\,f'(x).$$ Substitute $$f'(x)$$ from $$(2):$$ $$f''(x)=-\sec^{2}x\bigl(1+f(x)\bigr)-\tan x\bigl[-\tan x\,(1+f(x))\bigr].$$ Since $$\sec^{2}x=\tan^{2}x+1,$$ the bracket simplifies:
$$-\sec^{2}x+\tan^{2}x=-1.$$ Hence $$f''(x)=-(1+f(x))\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f''(x)+f(x)+1=0.\qquad -(3)$$

Step 4: Initial conditions.
From $$(1)$$ at $$x=0$$: $$f(0)=\ln\cos0=0.$$ From $$(2)$$ at $$x=0$$: $$f'(0)=-\tan0\,(1+f(0))=0.$$

Step 5: Solve the differential equation.
The homogeneous part of $$(3)$$ is $$f_h''+f_h=0,$$ giving $$f_h=C_1\cos x+C_2\sin x.$$ Seek a particular solution $$f_p=A$$ (constant). Substituting in $$(3)$$: $$0+A+1=0\;\Rightarrow\;A=-1.$$ Thus $$f(x)=C_1\cos x+C_2\sin x-1.$$ Apply the initial conditions: $$f(0)=C_1-1=0\;\Longrightarrow\;C_1=1,$$ $$f'(x)=-C_1\sin x+C_2\cos x,$$ so $$f'(0)=C_2=0.$$ Therefore $$f(x)=\cos x-1,\qquad f'(x)=-\sin x,\qquad f''(x)=-\cos x.$$

Step 6: Compute the required expression.
At $$x=\frac{\pi}{6}:$$ $$f\!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\cos\frac{\pi}{6}-1=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-1,$$ $$f''\!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.$$ At $$x=-\frac{\pi}{6}:$$ $$f'\!\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\sin\!\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac12.$$ Hence $$f''\!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+12\,f'\!\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+f\!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$$ $$=\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)+12\!\left(\frac12\right)+\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-1\right)= -\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+6+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-1=5.$$

Therefore the required value is 5.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Let

$$ f(x)=\int_0^x \tan (t-x)\,dt-\int_0^x f(t)\tan t\,dt, \qquad x\in \left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right). $$

We have to find

$$ f''\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+12f'\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right). $$

Step 1: Simplify the first integral

Consider

$$ \int_0^x \tan(t-x)\,dt. $$

Put

$$ u=t-x \implies du=dt. $$

When $t=0$, $u=-x$, and when $t=x$, $u=0$.

So,

$$ \int_0^x \tan(t-x)\,dt=\int_{-x}^0 \tan u\,du. $$

Now,

$$ \int \tan u\,du = -\ln(\cos u). $$

Hence,

$$ \int_{-x}^0 \tan u\,du = \left[-\ln(\cos u)\right]_{-x}^0 = -\ln(\cos 0)+\ln(\cos(-x)). $$

Since $\cos 0=1$ and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$,

$$ \int_0^x \tan(t-x)\,dt=\ln(\cos x). $$

Therefore the given equation becomes

$$ f(x)=\ln(\cos x)-\int_0^x f(t)\tan t\,dt. $$

So,

$$ f(x)+\int_0^x f(t)\tan t\,dt=\ln(\cos x). $$

Step 2: Differentiate the equation

Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$.

Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus,

$$ \frac{d}{dx}\left(\int_0^x f(t)\tan t\,dt\right)=f(x)\tan x. $$

Also,

$$ \frac{d}{dx}\big(\ln(\cos x)\big)= -\tan x. $$

Thus,

$$ f'(x)+f(x)\tan x=-\tan x. $$

So,

$$ f'(x)=-(f(x)+1)\tan x. $$

Step 3: Find $f(x)$ explicitly

Now observe that $f(x)=-1$ satisfies the differential equation:

$$ f'(x)=0,\qquad -(f(x)+1)\tan x=0. $$

Also from the original equation, put $x=0$:

$$ f(0)=\int_0^0 \tan(t-0)\,dt-\int_0^0 f(t)\tan t\,dt=0. $$

So,

$$ f(0)=0. $$

Let us solve the differential equation properly.

From

$$ f'(x)+(f(x)+1)\tan x=0, $$

put

$$ y(x)=f(x)+1. $$

Then

$$ y'(x)+y(x)\tan x=0. $$

This gives

$$ \frac{y'}{y}=-\tan x. $$

Integrating,

$$ \ln |y|=\int -\tan x\,dx=\ln(\cos x)+C. $$

Hence,

$$ y=C\cos x. $$

Therefore,

$$ f(x)+1=C\cos x. $$

Using $f(0)=0$,

$$ 0+1=C\cos 0=C. $$

So $C=1$, and hence

$$ f(x)+1=\cos x $$

which gives

$$ f(x)=\cos x-1. $$

Step 4: Find derivatives

Since

$$ f(x)=\cos x-1, $$

we get

$$ f'(x)=-\sin x, $$

and

$$ f''(x)=-\cos x. $$

Now compute required values:

1. $f''\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$

$$ f''\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. $$

2. $f'\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$

$$ f'\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) =\frac{1}{2}. $$

So,

$$ 12f'\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=12\cdot \frac{1}{2}=6. $$

3. $f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$

$$ f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)-1 =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1. $$

Step 5: Add them

$$ f''\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+12f'\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) $$

$$ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+6+\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1\right) $$

$$ = 6-1=5. $$

Hence, the required value is

$$ \boxed{5}. $$

subject: chemistry
question_text:
Match the List-I with List II

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
We recall the basic facts of photo-electric effect:
  • $$E = h\nu$$, where $$h$$ is Planck’s constant.
  • Einstein’s equation $$h\nu = \phi + eV_s$$, where
$$\phi$$ = work function (minimum energy required to eject an electron),
    $$V_s$$ = stopping potential, and
    $$e$$ = magnitude of electronic charge.
  • Threshold frequency $$\nu_0$$ satisfies $$h\nu_0 = \phi$$.





Let us evaluate the dimensions of each physical quantity.

Planck’s constant $$h$$
From $$E = h\nu$$ we have $$h = \dfrac{E}{\nu}$$.
Energy has dimensions $$[ML^2T^{-2}]$$ and frequency has $$[T^{-1}]$$.
Therefore
$$\left[h\right] = \dfrac{[ML^2T^{-2}]}{[T^{-1}]} = [ML^2T^{-1}]$$, which is set (III).



Stopping potential $$V_s$$
Potential (voltage) is work per unit charge: $$V = \dfrac{W}{Q}$$.
Work/energy has $$[ML^2T^{-2}]$$ and charge has $$[AT]$$ (since current $$I$$ has $$[A]$$ and $$Q = IT$$).
Hence
$$\left[V_s\right] = \dfrac{[ML^2T^{-2}]}{[AT]} = [ML^2T^{-3}A^{-1}]$$, which is set (IV).



Work function $$\phi$$
It is an energy, so
$$\left[\phi\right] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$$, which is set (I).

Threshold frequency $$\nu_0$$
Frequency is reciprocal of time, so
$$\left[\nu_0\right] = [T^{-1}]$$, which is set (II).

Collecting the matches:
A) Planck’s constant → (III) $$[ML^2T^{-1}]$$
B) Stopping potential → (IV) $$[ML^2T^{-3}A^{-1}]$$
C) Work function → (I) $$[ML^2T^{-2}]$$
D) Threshold frequency → (II) $$[T^{-1}]$$

This corresponds to Option A: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
A. Williamson Synthesis

In Williamson ether synthesis, an alkoxide ion attacks an alkyl halide and replaces the halogen.

So, it proceeds by nucleophilic substitution.

$$ A \rightarrow III $$

B. Friedel Craft Reaction

Friedel-Crafts reaction in benzene involves attack by an electrophile on the aromatic ring.

So, it is electrophilic substitution.

$$ B \rightarrow IV $$

C. Bromination of vinyl benzene

Vinyl benzene is styrene, having a double bond. Bromine adds across the double bond.

This is electrophilic addition.

$$ C \rightarrow I $$

D. Chlorination of toluene in light

In presence of light, chlorination of toluene occurs at the side chain by a radical pathway.

So, it is free radical substitution.

$$ D \rightarrow II $$

Therefore, the correct matching is:

$$ A-III,\; B-IV,\; C-I,\; D-II $$

So, the correct option is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option C}} $$

subject: physics
question_text: Two cars A and B move in the same direction along a straight line with speed $$100 km/h$$ and $$80 km/h$$, respectively such that  Car $$A$$ is moving ahead of Car $$B$$. A person in car B throws a stone with a speed $$v$$ so that it hit car $$A$$ with a speed of $$5$$ m/s. The value of  $$v$$ is ________ $$km/h$$ :

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Let the speeds with respect to the ground be:

Car A : $$u_A = 100$$ km/h
Car B : $$u_B = 80$$ km/h

A passenger sitting in car B throws the stone straight ahead with speed $$v$$ relative to car B. Hence the speed of the stone with respect to the ground is

$$u_s = u_B + v \quad$$ (because both the car and the throw are in the same direction).

The stone must hit car A with a relative speed (speed of approach) of $$5$$ m/s. Therefore, in ground frame, the relative speed between the stone and car A is

$$u_{\text{rel}} = u_s - u_A = (u_B + v) - u_A.$$

This relative speed should equal $$5$$ m/s. First convert $$5$$ m/s to km/h:

$$5\;\text{m/s} = 5 \times \frac{18}{5} = 18 \;\text{km/h}.$$

Set up the equation

$$u_{\text{rel}} = 18$$
$$\Longrightarrow (u_B + v) - u_A = 18$$
$$\Longrightarrow (80 + v) - 100 = 18$$

Solving for $$v$$:

$$v - 20 = 18 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = 38 \;\text{km/h}.$$

Hence the required throwing speed is

Option C which is: 38 km/h.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The velocity of car $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{A}}=100 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$

The velocity of car $\mathrm{B}, \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{B}}=80 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$

The stone hits car $A$ with speed $5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, i.e., relative speed with which the stone hits car $A, \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{SA}}=5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

The stone is thrown with speed v , i.e., the relative speed of the stone relative to car B is $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{SB}}=\mathrm{v}$

The final speed is given in $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$, but we need to find the value of v in in $\mathrm{km} / \mathrm{h}$.

$$ \frac{1 \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{~s}}=\frac{18}{5} \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h} $$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{SA}}=5 \times \frac{18}{5}=18 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h} \ldots$ (i)

When the person in car B throws the stone with speed v relative to the car, the actual velocity of the stone with respect to the ground $\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}}\right)$ is the sum of the car's velocity and the throw velocity:

$$ v_{S B}=v_S-v_B=v \Rightarrow v_s=v_B+v \ldots (ii) $$

The stone hits car $A$ with a relative speed $v_{S A}$. The relative velocity of the stone with respect to car $A$ is:

$$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{SA}}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{S}}-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}} .....(iii)$$

Substituting the expression for $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}$ from equation (ii) :

$$ v_{S A}=\left(v_B+v\right)-v_A $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{v}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{sA}}+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}} $$

Substituting the values :

$$ \mathrm{v}=18+100-80 $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{v}=18+20$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{v}=38 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h} $$

Therefore, the value of $v$ is $38 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

subject: physics
question_text: At $$t = 0$$, a body of mass $$100$$ g starts moving under the influence of a force $$(5\hat{i} + 10\hat{j})$$ N. After $$2$$ s, its  position is $$(2x\hat{i} + 5y\hat{j})$$ m. The ratio $$x : y$$ is ______.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The mass of the body is given in grams, so first convert it into SI units:
$$m = 100\,\text{g} = 0.1\,\text{kg}$$

The constant force acting on the body is
$$\mathbf{F} = 5\hat{i} + 10\hat{j}\,\text{N}$$

Using Newton’s second law $$\mathbf{F}=m\mathbf{a}$$, the acceleration components are

$$a_x = \frac{5}{0.1} = 50\,\text{m\,s}^{-2}$$
$$a_y = \frac{10}{0.1} = 100\,\text{m\,s}^{-2}$$

The question does not state any initial velocity, so we take the body to start from rest at $$t = 0$$:
$$u_x = 0,\; u_y = 0$$.

For motion with constant acceleration, the displacement after time $$t$$ in each direction is
$$s = ut + \tfrac12 a t^2$$.

Time interval: $$t = 2\,\text{s}$$.

Along the $$x$$-axis:
Displacement is given as $$2x$$, so
$$2x = \tfrac12 a_x t^2$$
$$2x = \tfrac12 \times 50 \times (2)^2$$
$$2x = 0.5 \times 50 \times 4 = 100$$
$$x = 50$$.

Along the $$y$$-axis:
Displacement is given as $$5y$$, so
$$5y = \tfrac12 a_y t^2$$
$$5y = \tfrac12 \times 100 \times (2)^2$$
$$5y = 0.5 \times 100 \times 4 = 200$$
$$y = 40$$.

Therefore, the required ratio is
$$x : y = 50 : 40 = 5 : 4$$.

Hence the correct choice is:
Option D which is: $$5:4$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The mass of the body, $\mathrm{m}=100 \mathrm{~g}=0.1 \mathrm{~kg}$

The constant force acting on the body, $\vec{F}=(5 \hat{\imath}+10 \hat{\jmath}) N$

The time interval of motion, $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}$

As the body started from rest, so the initial velocity at $\mathrm{t}=0, \overrightarrow{\mathrm{u}}=0$

The position at $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}, \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}=(2 \mathrm{xi}+5 \mathrm{y}) \mathrm{j}) \mathrm{m}$

According to Newton's Second Law of Motion :

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{m} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}}{\mathrm{~m}} $$

Substituting the values :

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{5 \hat{\imath}+10 \hat{\jmath}}{0.1} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=(50 \hat{\imath}+100 \hat{\jmath}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^2 $$

From the second equation of motion for constant acceleration:

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{ut}}+\frac{1}{2} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} t^2 $$

Since $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{u}}=0$ :

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{1}{2} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{t}^2 $$

Substituting the acceleration and time :

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{1}{2}(50 \hat{\imath}+100 \hat{\jmath})(2)^2 $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{1}{2}(50 \hat{\imath}+100 \hat{\jmath})(4)$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\vec{s}=2(50 \hat{\imath}+100 \hat{\jmath})$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}=(100 i \hat{\imath}+200 \hat{\jmath}) \mathrm{m}$

On comparing the calculated displacement with the given position $(2 x \hat{i}+5 y \hat{j})$ :

For the x -component: $2 \mathrm{x}=100 \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=50$

For the $y$-component: $5 y=200 \Rightarrow y=40$

So, the required ratio is,

$$ \frac{x}{y}=\frac{50}{40}=5: 4 $$

Therefore, the ratio $\mathrm{x}: \mathrm{y}$ is $5: 4$.

Thus, the correct option is (D).

subject: physics
question_text: If x and y coordinates of a projectile as a function of time (t) are given as $$24t$$ and $$43.6t - 4.9t^2$$, respectively, then the angle (in degrees) made by the projectile with horizontal when $$t = 2$$ s is ______.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The position of the projectile is given as a function of time:

$$x = 24t, \quad y = 43.6t - 4.9t^{2}$$

The instantaneous velocity components are obtained by differentiating the position coordinates with respect to time.

Horizontal component: $$v_x = \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{d(24t)}{dt} = 24 \text{ m\,s}^{-1}$$

Vertical component: $$v_y = \frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{d\bigl(43.6t - 4.9t^{2}\bigr)}{dt} = 43.6 - 9.8t \text{ m\,s}^{-1}$$

At $$t = 2$$ s, substitute in the expressions above:

$$v_x = 24 \text{ m\,s}^{-1}$$ (constant for all $$t$$)
$$v_y = 43.6 - 9.8(2) = 43.6 - 19.6 = 24 \text{ m\,s}^{-1}$$

The angle $$\theta$$ that the velocity vector makes with the horizontal is given by

$$\tan\theta = \frac{v_y}{v_x} = \frac{24}{24} = 1$$

Therefore, $$\theta = 45^{\circ}$$.

Hence, the correct choice is:
Option B which is: $$45°$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Horizontal position of projectile is given as $\mathrm{x}=24 \mathrm{t}$

Vertical position of projectile is given as $\mathrm{y}=43.6 \mathrm{t}-4.9 \mathrm{t}^2$

Velocity is the rate of change of position with respect to time $\left(\vec{V}=\frac{d \vec{r}}{d t}\right)$.

For the velocity component along horizontal, $\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{x}}\right)$ :

$$ v_x=\frac{d x}{d t}=\frac{d}{d t}(24 t)=24 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$

The horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the motion.

For the velocity component along vertical, $\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}\right)$ :

$$ v_y=\frac{d y}{d t}=\frac{d}{d t}\left(43.6 t-4.9 t^2\right) $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}=43.6-(2 \times 4.9) \mathrm{t}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ v_y=43.6-9.8 t $$

So, the velocities at $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}$ is,

$$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{x}}=24 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}=43.6-9.8(2)=43.6-19.6=24 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$

The angle $\theta$ that the velocity vector makes with the horizontal is given by

$$ \tan \theta=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{x}}} $$

Substituting the values calculated for $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}$ :

$$ \tan \theta=\frac{24}{24} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\tan \theta=1$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \theta=45^{\circ} $$

Therefore, the angle made by the projectile with the horizontal at $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}$ is $45^{\circ}$.

Thus, the correct option is (B).

subject: physics
question_text: The height in terms of radius of the earth (R), at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes $$\frac{g}{9}$$, where g is acceleration due to gravity on earth's surface, is ______.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Acceleration due to gravity at a height $$h$$ above Earth’s surface is given by
$$g_h = \frac{g}{\left(1 + \frac{h}{R}\right)^{2}}$$

The question states that this value becomes $$\dfrac{g}{9}$$, so set
$$\frac{g}{\left(1 + \frac{h}{R}\right)^{2}} = \frac{g}{9}$$

Cancel $$g$$ from both sides:
$$\left(1 + \frac{h}{R}\right)^{2} = 9$$

Take the positive square root (height is positive):
$$1 + \frac{h}{R} = 3$$

Solve for $$h$$:
$$\frac{h}{R} = 3 - 1 = 2$$
$$h = 2R$$

The required height is $$2R$$.

Option C which is: $$2R$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
According to Newton's Law of universal gravitation, the acceleration due to gravity ( $g$ ) on the surface of Earth is,

$$ g=\frac{G M}{R^2} \ldots \text { (i) } $$

Where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $M$ is the mass of the Earth, and $R$ is the radius of the Earth.

If the body is placed at a height h above the Earth's surface, its total distance from the centre of the Earth becomes $(\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h})$. The acceleration due to gravity at this height is:

$$ \mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{GM}}{(\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h})^2}...... (ii) $$

Dividing equation (ii) by equation (i) :

$$ \frac{\mathrm{g}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{g}}=\frac{\mathrm{GM} /(\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h})^2}{\mathrm{GM} / \mathrm{R}^2} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{g^{\prime}}{g}=\frac{R^2}{(R+h)^2}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\mathrm{g}\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h}}\right)^2 $$

It is given that the acceleration due to gravity at height h is $\mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{g}}{9}$ :

$$ \frac{g}{9}=g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2 $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{9}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h}}\right)^2$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{1}{3}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h}=3 \mathrm{R} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~h}=2 \mathrm{R} $$

Therefore, the height at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes $\frac{g}{9}$ is $2 R$.

Thus, the correct option is (C).

subject: physics
question_text: A metal string A is suspended from a rigid support and its free end is attached to a block of mass M. Second block having mass 2M is suspended at the bottom of the first block using a string B. The area of cross sections of strings A and B are same. The ratio of lengths of strings of A to B is 2 and the ratio of their Young's moduli $$(Y_A/Y_B)$$ is 0.5. The ratio of elongations in A to B is ______.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Both strings have the same cross-sectional area, call it $$A$$. The masses of the strings themselves are negligible, so the only forces are the weights of the attached masses.

For string B
Only the mass $$2M$$ is hanging from its lower end, so the tension throughout string B is
$$F_B = 2Mg$$

For string A
String A has to support both masses: the mass $$M$$ fixed to its lower end and the mass $$2M$$ hanging further below. Hence the tension in string A is
$$F_A = (M + 2M)g = 3Mg$$

The elongation of a string of length $$L$$ under tension $$F$$ is given by
$$\Delta L = \frac{F\,L}{A\,Y}$$
where $$Y$$ is Young’s modulus.

Let the original lengths be $$L_A$$ and $$L_B$$. The data give
$$\frac{L_A}{L_B} = 2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad L_A = 2L_B$$
and
$$\frac{Y_A}{Y_B} = 0.5 \quad\Rightarrow\quad Y_B = 2Y_A$$

Now write the ratio of elongations:

$$\frac{\Delta L_A}{\Delta L_B} = \frac{\dfrac{F_A L_A}{A Y_A}} {\dfrac{F_B L_B}{A Y_B}} = \frac{F_A L_A Y_B}{F_B L_B Y_A}$$

Insert the known values:

$$\frac{\Delta L_A}{\Delta L_B} = \frac{(3Mg)\,(2L_B)\,(2Y_A)}{(2Mg)\,(L_B)\,(Y_A)} = \frac{3 \times 2 \times 2}{2} = 6$$

Therefore, the ratio of elongations is $$\mathbf{6}$$.

Option D which is: $$6$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Young's Modulus (Y) is defined as the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain :

$$ \mathrm{Y}=\frac{\text { Stress }}{\text { Strain }}=\frac{\mathrm{F} / \mathrm{A}}{\Delta \mathrm{~L} / \mathrm{L}} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Delta \mathrm{L}=\frac{\mathrm{FL}}{\mathrm{AY}} \ldots (ii)$$

Where, F is the tension in the string, L is the original length, A is the area of cross-section. Y is the Young's Modulus.

For string B

This string supports only the bottom block of mass 2 M .

$$ \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}}=2 \mathrm{Mg} $$

For string A

This string supports both mass M and the mass 2 M hanging below it.

$$ \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{Mg}+2 \mathrm{Mg}=3 \mathrm{Mg} $$

The ratio of lengths is $\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=2$

The ratio of Young's moduli is $\frac{\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{B}}}=0.5$.

The areas are same, $A_A=A_B=A$.

Using the formula of extension in string (i),

$$ \frac{\Delta L_A}{\Delta L_B}=\frac{F_A L_A / A_A Y_A}{F_B L_B / A_B Y_B}=\left(\frac{F_A}{F_B}\right) \times\left(\frac{L_A}{L_B}\right)\left(\frac{Y_B}{Y_A}\right) $$

Substituting the values :

$$ \frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{Mg}}{2 \mathrm{Mg}}\right) \times(2) \times\left(\frac{1}{0.5}\right) $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) \times 2 \times 2$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=3 \times 2=6 $$

Therefore, the ratio of elongations in A to B is 6.

Thus, the correct option is (D).

subject: physics
question_text: A water spray gun is attached to a hose of cross sectional area 30 cm$$^2$$. The gun comprises of 10 perforations each of cross sectional area of 15 mm$$^2$$. If the water flows in the hose with the speed of 50 cm/s, calculate the speed at which the water flows out from each perforation. (Neglect any edge effects)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The volume flow rate of an incompressible fluid remains constant along a streamline. This is the equation of continuity: $$Q = A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$, where $$Q$$ is the discharge (volume per time), $$A$$ is area and $$v$$ is speed.

Inlet (hose)
Cross-sectional area: $$30\text{ cm}^2 = 30 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2 = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2$$
Speed of water: $$50\text{ cm/s} = 0.50\text{ m/s}$$

Volume flow rate at inlet:
$$Q = A_{\text{in}} v_{\text{in}} = (3.0 \times 10^{-3}) (0.50) = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3\!\!/\text{s}$$

Outlet (10 perforations)
Area of one perforation: $$15\text{ mm}^2 = 15 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2$$
Total outlet area: $$A_{\text{out}} = 10 \times 15 \times 10^{-6} = 1.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$$

Let $$v_{\text{out}}$$ be the speed of water emerging from each perforation (all equal). Using continuity: $$Q = A_{\text{out}} v_{\text{out}}$$

Therefore,
$$v_{\text{out}} = \frac{Q}{A_{\text{out}}} = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{-3}}{1.5 \times 10^{-4}} = 10\text{ m/s}$$

Hence, the speed of water leaving each perforation is $$10\text{ m/s}$$.

Option B which is: $$10\text{ m/s}$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
For an incompressible fluid, the volume of fluid entering a pipe per unit time must equal the volume of fluid leaving the pipe per unit time.

Volume Flow Rate (In) = Volume Flow Rate (Out)

$$ A_1 v_1=A_2 v_2 $$

Where A is the area and v is the velocity of the fluid.

The area of hose is $\mathrm{A}_1=30 \mathrm{~cm}^2=30 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2$.

The speed in hose is $\mathrm{v}_1=50 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}=0.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

Number of perforations is $\mathrm{n}=10$.

The area of one perforation is $\mathrm{a}=15 \mathrm{~mm}^2=15 \times\left(10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}\right)^2=15 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^2$

So, total area of exit is, $\mathrm{A}_2=\mathrm{n} \times \mathrm{a}=10 \times 15 \times 10^{-6}=150 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^2$

Using the equation of continuity:

$$ A_1 v_1=A_2 v_2 $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ v_2=\frac{A_1 v_1}{A_2} $$

Substituting the values :

$$ v_2=\frac{\left(30 \times 10^{-4}\right) \times 0.5}{150 \times 10^{-6}} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $v_2=\frac{15 \times 10^{-4}}{150 \times 10^{-6}}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{v}_2=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$

Therefore, the speed at which the water flows out from each perforation is $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

Thus, the correct option is (B).

subject: physics
question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R

Assertion A: If the average kinetic energy of H$$_2$$ and O$$_2$$ molecules, kept in two different sized containers are same, then their temperatures will be same.

Reason R: The r.m.s. speed of H$$_2$$ and O$$_2$$ molecules are same at same temperature.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Average translational kinetic energy per molecule in an ideal gas is given by
$$\overline{E_k} = \frac{3}{2}kT$$
where $$k$$ is Boltzmann’s constant and $$T$$ is the absolute temperature.

Thus, when $$\overline{E_k}$$ of any two gases is equal, we must have the same temperature $$T$$ for both. Therefore, the Assertion (A) is true.

The rms speed of molecules of an ideal gas is
$$v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3kT}{m}}$$
where $$m$$ is the mass of one molecule (or molar mass $$M$$ in suitable units). For two different gases at the same temperature:
$$\frac{v_{\text{rms}(1)}}{v_{\text{rms}(2)}} = \sqrt{\frac{m_2}{m_1}}$$

Because $$m_{H_2} \neq m_{O_2}$$, their rms speeds cannot be equal at the same temperature. Hence the Reason (R) is false.

Assertion is true while Reason is false ⇒ Option C.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
According to the kinetic theory of gases, the average translational kinetic energy ( $\mathrm{K}_{\text {avg }}$ ) of a gas molecule is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (T).

$$ \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{~T} $$

Where $\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the Boltzmann constant.

So, the average kinetic energy depends only on the temperature and not on the mass of the molecule or the size/volume of the container.

Since $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{avg}}$ is the same for both $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{O}_2$, their temperatures (T) must be identical.

Therefore, Assertion A is true.

The root mean square (r. m. s.) speed ( $\mathrm{v}_{\text {rms }}$ ) of a gas molecule is given by the formula:

$$ v_{r m s}=\sqrt{\frac{3 R T}{M}} $$

Where R is the universal gas constant, T is the absolute temperature, and M is the molar mass of the gas.

At the same temperature (T), $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}}$ is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass (M).

Since the molar mass of $\mathrm{H}_2(2 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol})$ is different from $\mathrm{O}_2(32 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol})$, their r.m.s. speeds will be different even at the same temperature.

Therefore, Reason R is false.

Hence, Assertion A is true, but Reason R is false.

So, the correct option is (C).

subject: physics
question_text: The temperature of a metal strip having coefficient of linear expansion $$\alpha$$ is increased from $$T_1$$ to $$T_2$$ resulting in increase of its length by $$\Delta L_1$$. The temperature is further increased from $$T_2$$ to $$T_3$$ such that the increase in its length is $$\Delta L_2$$. Given $$T_3 + T_1 = 2T_2$$ and $$T_2 - T_1 = \Delta T$$, the value of $$\Delta L_2$$ is ______.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Let the original length of the strip at temperature $$T_1$$ be $$L_0$$. For a solid with constant linear expansion coefficient $$\alpha$$, the change in length for a temperature change $$\Delta T$$ is

$$\Delta L = L \,\alpha\,\Delta T \quad -(1)$$

Elongation from $$T_1$$ to $$T_2$$
The temperature rise is $$T_2-T_1 = \Delta T$$. Using $$(1)$$ with the initial length $$L_0$$, we have

$$\Delta L_1 = L_0 \,\alpha\,\Delta T \quad -(2)$$

After this heating, the new length at $$T_2$$ becomes

$$L_{T_2} = L_0 + \Delta L_1 = L_0\bigl(1+\alpha\Delta T\bigr) \quad -(3)$$

Elongation from $$T_2$$ to $$T_3$$
We are told $$T_3+T_1 = 2T_2$$. Re-arranging, $$T_3 - T_2 = T_2 - T_1 = \Delta T \quad -(4)$$ Thus the second heating also raises the temperature by $$\Delta T$$.

Now use $$(1)$$ again, but the initial length for this stage is $$L_{T_2}$$ from $$(3)$$:

$$\Delta L_2 = L_{T_2}\,\alpha\,(T_3-T_2) = L_0\bigl(1+\alpha\Delta T\bigr)\alpha\Delta T \quad -(5)$$

Compare $$(5)$$ with $$(2)$$ (note that $$\Delta L_1 = L_0\alpha\Delta T$$):

$$\Delta L_2 = \Delta L_1\bigl(1+\alpha\Delta T\bigr)$$

Hence

$$\boxed{\;\Delta L_2 = \Delta L_1[\,1+\alpha\Delta T\,]\;}$$

Therefore the correct option is
Option D which is: $$\Delta L_1[1 + \alpha\Delta T]$$.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
When a metal of length $L$ having coefficient of linear expansion $\alpha$ is heated by temperature $\Delta T$, then the change in length is given as $\Delta \mathrm{L}=\mathrm{L} \alpha \Delta \mathrm{T}$

For the first interval of heating $\left(\mathrm{T}_1 \rightarrow \mathrm{~T}_2\right)$ :

The increase in length $\Delta \mathrm{L}_1$ is given by $\Delta \mathrm{L}_1=\mathrm{L}_1 \alpha\left(\mathrm{~T}_2-\mathrm{T}_1\right)$

It is given that $\mathrm{T}_2-\mathrm{T}_1=\Delta \mathrm{T}$ :

$$ \Delta \mathrm{L}_1=\mathrm{L}_1 \alpha \Delta \mathrm{~T} .....(i) $$

The new length at temperature $\mathrm{T}_2$ is:

$$ \mathrm{L}_2=\mathrm{L}_1+\Delta \mathrm{L}_1=\mathrm{L}_1(1+\alpha \Delta \mathrm{T}) ........(ii)$$

For the second interval of heating, ( $\mathrm{T}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{~T}_3$ )

The increase in length is $\Delta \mathrm{L}_2$ depends on the length at the start of this stage $\left(\mathrm{L}_2\right)$ :

$$ \Delta \mathrm{L}_2=\mathrm{L}_2 \alpha\left(\mathrm{~T}_3-\mathrm{T}_2\right) $$

From the given condition $\mathrm{T}_3+\mathrm{T}_1=2 \mathrm{~T}_2$ :

$$ \mathrm{T}_3-\mathrm{T}_2=\mathrm{T}_2-\mathrm{T}_1 $$

Since $\mathrm{T}_2-\mathrm{T}_1=\Delta \mathrm{T}$, then $\mathrm{T}_3-\mathrm{T}_2=\Delta \mathrm{T}$.

Substituting this into the $\Delta \mathrm{L}_2$ formula:

$$\Delta \mathrm{L}_2=\mathrm{L}_2 \alpha \Delta \mathrm{~T}.......(iii) $$

Substitute the value of $\mathrm{L}_2$ from equation (ii) into equation (iii) :

$$ \Delta \mathrm{L}_2=\left[\mathrm{L}_1(1+\alpha \Delta \mathrm{T})\right] \alpha \Delta \mathrm{T} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Delta \mathrm{L}_2=\left(\mathrm{L}_1 \alpha \Delta \mathrm{~T}\right)(1+\alpha \Delta \mathrm{T}) $$

From equation (i), we know $\mathrm{L}_1 \alpha \Delta \mathrm{~T}=\Delta \mathrm{L}_1$.

$$ \Delta \mathrm{L}_2=\Delta \mathrm{L}_1(1+\alpha \Delta \mathrm{T}) $$

Therefore, the value of $\Delta L_2$ is $\Delta L_1[1+\alpha \Delta T]$.

Thus, the correct option is (D).

subject: physics
question_text: A uniform disc of radius R and mass M is free to oscillate about the axis A as shown in the figure. For small oscillations the time period is ______. ( g is acceleration due to gravity)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
For small-angle oscillations about a fixed horizontal axis, any rigid body behaves as a physical pendulum. Its time period is

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I_A}{Mgd}} \quad -(1)$$
where
  • $$I_A$$ is the moment of inertia about the axis of suspension A,
  • $$M$$ is the mass of the body,
  • $$d$$ is the distance between the axis A and the centre of mass (C.O.M.),
  • $$g$$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Moment of inertia about axis A

The disc is uniform, has radius $$R$$ and mass $$M$$. The axis A passes through a point on the rim and is perpendicular to the plane of the disc (a tangential axis). Using the parallel-axis theorem,

$$I_A = I_{\text{cm dia}} + Md^{2} \quad -(2)$$
Here,
  • $$I_{\text{cm dia}}$$ for a disc about its central axis (parallel to the plane) is $$\frac{1}{4}MR^{2}$$.
  • The distance from the rim to the centre is $$d = R$$.

Substitute in $$(2):$$

$$I_A = \frac{1}{4}MR^{2} \;+\; M R^{2} \;=\; \frac{5}{4} M R^{2} \quad -(3)$$

Distance $$d$$ between axis and C.O.M.

The C.O.M. of a uniform disc is at its centre, so $$d = R$$.

Time period

Insert $$I_A$$ from $$(3)$$ and $$d = R$$ into the physical-pendulum formula $$(1):$$

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\frac{5}{4}MR^{2}}{M g R}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}\,\frac{R}{g}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{5R}{4g}}$$

Thus the time period of oscillation is

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{5R}{4g}}$$

Option A which is: $$2\pi\sqrt{\frac{5R}{4g}}$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
For a physical pendulum that oscillates about a horizontal axis. For a small angular displacement $\theta$, the restoring torque $\tau$ is:

$$ \tau=-\mathrm{Mgd} \sin \theta $$

For small angular displacement $\sin \theta \approx \theta$

$$ \Rightarrow \tau \approx-\operatorname{Mgd} \theta $$

Where d is the distance from the pivot A to the centre of mass.

Since $\tau=\mathrm{I} \alpha=\mathrm{I} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \theta}{\mathrm{dt}^2}$, where I is the moment of inertia about the pivot:

$$ \mathrm{I} \frac{\mathrm{~d}^2 \theta}{\mathrm{dt}^2}+\operatorname{Mgd} \theta=0 \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{~d}^2 \theta}{\mathrm{dt}^2}+\left(\frac{\mathrm{Mgd}}{\mathrm{I}}\right) \theta=0 $$

This is the equation for SHM with $\omega^2=\frac{\mathrm{Mgd}}{\mathrm{I}}$.

So, the time period T of oscillation is:

$$ \mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{Mgd}}} $$

The axis of rotation A is at the edge of the disc.

The moment of inertia of a uniform disc about its centre of mass (axis perpendicular to the plane) is,

$$ \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{MR}^2 $$

Using perpendicular axis theorem, if the moment of inertia about diameter of ring is $I_d$ then

$I_{\mathrm{cm}}=I_{\mathrm{z}}=I_{\mathrm{x}}+I_{\mathrm{y}}=I_{\mathrm{d}}+I_{\mathrm{d}} \Rightarrow I_{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{I_{\mathrm{z}}}{2}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{cm}}}{2}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{MR}^2}{2}=\frac{1}{4} \mathrm{MR}^2 $$

Now, the given axis is parallel to the diameter. So, sing the parallel axis theorem $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{cm}}+\mathrm{Md}^2$ Since the pivot A is at a distance $\mathrm{d}=\mathrm{R}$ from the centre :

$$ \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{1}{4} \mathrm{MR}^2+\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{R})^2 $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{5}{4} \mathrm{MR}^2 $$

The distance from the pivot $A$ to the centre of mass is $d=R$.

Substituting $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and d into the time period formula :

$$ \mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\frac{5}{4} \mathrm{MR}^2}{\mathrm{MgR}}} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{5 \mathrm{R}}{4 \mathrm{~g}}} $$

Therefore, the time period for small oscillations is $2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{5 \mathrm{R}}{4 \mathrm{~g}}}$.

Thus, the correct option is (A).

subject: physics
question_text: A rigid dipole undergoes a simple harmonic motion about its centre in the presence of an electric field $$\vec{E}_1 = E_0\hat{x}$$. If another electric field $$\vec{E}_2 = 2E_0(\hat{y} + \hat{z})$$ is introduced to the system, what will be the percentage change in the frequency of the oscillation (approximate)?

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The restoring torque on a rigid electric dipole of moment magnitude $$p$$ kept in a uniform field $$\vec E$$ is $$\tau = -pE\sin\theta$$, where $$\theta$$ is the small angular displacement from the equilibrium direction.

For small oscillations $$\sin\theta \approx \theta$$, so the equation of rotational SHM is

$$I\frac{d^{2}\theta}{dt^{2}} = -pE\,\theta$$

Here $$I$$ is the moment of inertia of the dipole about its axis of rotation. Comparing with $$\ddot\theta + \omega^{2}\theta = 0$$, the angular frequency is

$$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{pE}{I}}$$

Case 1: Only the original field $$\vec{E}_1 = E_0\hat x$$ is present.
Magnitude $$E_1 = E_0$$

$$\omega_1 = \sqrt{\frac{pE_0}{I}}$$

Case 2: The additional field $$\vec{E}_2 = 2E_0(\hat y + \hat z)$$ is switched on.

The net field is the vector sum

$$\vec E_{\text{net}} = E_0\hat x + 2E_0\hat y + 2E_0\hat z$$

Magnitude

$$E_{\text{net}} = E_0\sqrt{1^{2} + 2^{2} + 2^{2}} = E_0\sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3E_0$$

The new angular frequency is therefore

$$\omega_2 = \sqrt{\frac{pE_{\text{net}}}{I}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(3E_0)}{I}} = \sqrt{3}\,\omega_1$$

The ordinary (cyclic) frequency is proportional to angular frequency, so the same factor applies:

$$f_2 = \sqrt{3}\,f_1$$

Percentage change in frequency:

$$\frac{f_2 - f_1}{f_1}\times 100\% = (\sqrt{3}-1)\times 100\% \approx (1.732 - 1)\times 100\% \approx 0.732 \times 100\% \approx 73\%$$

Hence, the frequency increases by approximately $$73\%$$.

Option A which is: $$73\%$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
When a dipole with dipole moment $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}$ is placed in an electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$, the restoring torque is $\vec{\tau}=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$

The magnitude of restoring torque is $\tau=-\mathrm{pE} \sin \theta$.

For small $\theta$,

$$ \tau \approx-\text { pEÎ¸ } $$

The equation of motion is $\mathrm{I} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \theta}{\mathrm{dt}^2}=-\mathrm{pE} \theta$, where I is the moment of inertia.

The angular frequency is $\omega=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{pE}}{\mathrm{I}}}$, so the frequency f is:

$$ f=\frac{\omega}{2 \pi} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{f}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{pE}}{\mathrm{I}}}$

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{f} \propto \sqrt{\mathrm{E}}$

Where E is the magnitude of the net electric field.

Initial electric field is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_1=\mathrm{E}_0 \widehat{\mathrm{x}}$.

Magnitude of initial electric field is $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{E}_0$.

The additional electric field is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_2=2 \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{y}}+2 \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{z}}$.

So, the net electric field is

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{net}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_1+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_2=\mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{x}}+2 \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{y}}+2 \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{z}} $$

Magnitude of the net electric field is,

$$ \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{net}}=\sqrt{\left(\mathrm{E}_0\right)^2+\left(2 \mathrm{E}_0\right)^2+\left(2 \mathrm{E}_0\right)^2}=\sqrt{\mathrm{E}_0^2+4 \mathrm{E}_0^2+4 \mathrm{E}_0^2} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{net}}=\sqrt{9 \mathrm{E}_0^2}=3 \mathrm{E}_0 $$

Let $f_1$ be the initial frequency and $f_2$ be the final frequency.

$$ \frac{\mathrm{f}_2}{\mathrm{f}_1}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{f}}}{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{i}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{E}_0}{\mathrm{E}_0}}=\sqrt{3} \approx 1.732 $$

So, the percentage change is

$$ \Delta \%=\left(\frac{\mathrm{f}_2-\mathrm{f}_1}{\mathrm{f}_1}\right) \times 100 $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\Delta \%=(\sqrt{3}-1) \times 100$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Delta \%=(1.732-1) \times 100=0.732 \times 100=73.2 \% $$

Therefore, the approximate percentage change in the frequency of oscillation is $73 \%$.

Thus, the correct option is (A).

subject: physics
question_text:
From the circuit given below, the capacitance between terminals A and B shown in the circuit is ______ $$\mu$$F.
(take $$C_1 = C_2 = C_3 = 1$$ $$\mu$$F and $$C_4 = 2$$ $$\mu$$F.)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Let the node between $$C_1$$ and $$C_2$$ be P. 
The node between $$C_2$$ and $$C_3$$ is A (since that is shorted)
The two capacitors $$C_1 , C_2 $$ are connected end-to-end between the terminals A and P, so they are in parallel.
The simplified circuit looks like 

$$(C_1 \parallel C_2) \text{ in series with } C_4$$
$$\text{and the above eq. cap in parallel with } C_3$$

$$C_{eq} = \frac{(C_1 + C_2)C_4}{(C_1 + C_2) + C_4} + C_3$$

$$= \frac{(1 + 1)(2)}{1 + 1 + 2} + 1$$

$$= \frac{4}{4} + 1$$

$$= 2\mu F$$

Option C which is: $$2,\mu F$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Let the node between $\mathrm{C}_1$ and $\mathrm{C}_2$ be X ,

The wire (short circuit) connecting terminal A to node between $\mathrm{C}_2$ and $\mathrm{C}_3$. Thus, this node is at the same potential as A.

So, capacitor $\mathrm{C}_1$ is connected between A and X .

The capacitor $\mathrm{C}_2$ is connected between A and X .

The capacitor $C_3$ is connected between $A$ and $B$.

The capacitor $\mathrm{C}_4$ is connected between X and B .

So, the simplified circuit is,

Given values of capacitances are, $\mathrm{C}_1=1 \mu \mathrm{~F}, \mathrm{C}_2=1 \mu \mathrm{~F}, \mathrm{C}_3=1 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ and $\mathrm{C}_4=2 \mu \mathrm{~F}$

Both $\mathrm{C}_1$ and $\mathrm{C}_2$ are connected between point A and point X in parallel.

The equivalent capacitance $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{AX}}$ is :

$$ C_{A X}=C_1+C_2 $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ C_{A X}=1 \mu F+1 \mu F=2 \mu F $$

Now, the combination $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{AX}}$ is in series with $\mathrm{C}_4$ because the charge must flow through $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{AX}}$ to reach $\mathrm{C}_4$. So, the equivalent capacitance ( $\mathrm{C}^{\prime}$ ) is

$$ \frac{1}{\mathrm{C}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{AX}}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_4} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{C}^{\prime}=1 \mu \mathrm{~F} $$

The entire top branch ( $C^{\prime}$ ) is now in parallel with $C_3$, as both are connected across the main terminals $A$ and $B$.

The total equivalent capacitance $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is :

$$ C_{\mathrm{eq}}=C^{\prime}+C_3 $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{eq}}=1 \mu \mathrm{~F}+1 \mu \mathrm{~F}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{eq}}=2 \mu \mathrm{~F} $$

Therefore, the equivalent capacitance between A and B is $2 \mu \mathrm{~F}$.

Thus, the correct option is (A).

subject: physics
question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R

Assertion A: In electrostatics, a conductor does not store any net charge inside.

Reason R: Inside the capacitor (with no dielectric medium), the free charge carriers, if placed between the plates of capacitor, experience force and drift.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The assertion states: “A conductor has no net charge inside it.”

In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field $$\mathbf{E}$$ inside a conductor is zero. By Gauss’s law, $$\oint \mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{A}= \frac{Q_{\text{encl}}}{\varepsilon_0}$$. Since $$\mathbf{E}=0$$ everywhere on the Gaussian surface drawn wholly inside the conductor, the left side is zero, giving $$Q_{\text{encl}} = 0$$. Hence no net charge can reside in the interior; all excess charge moves to the outer surface. Therefore the Assertion (A) is true.

The reason says: “Inside a parallel plate capacitor (without dielectric), free charges experience a force and drift.” Between the plates of an isolated parallel-plate capacitor there exists a uniform electric field $$\mathbf{E} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$$ (directed from positive to negative plate). Any free charge placed in this region will indeed feel the force $$\mathbf{F}=q\mathbf{E}$$ and will drift toward one of the plates. Hence the Reason (R) is also true.

However, the phenomenon of charge drift inside the gap of a capacitor explains the behaviour of charges in a region where a finite electric field already exists; it does not account for the absence of net charge inside a conductor, which follows from zero electric field and Gauss’s law as shown above. Thus R is not the correct explanation of A.

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A. Hence the correct choice is:

Option B which is: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor is zero $(\mathrm{E}=0)$.

According to Gauss's Law $\left(\oint \mathrm{E} \cdot \mathrm{dA}=\frac{\mathrm{q}_{\text {in }}}{\epsilon_0}\right)$, if the electric field is zero everywhere inside, the net charge enclosed ( $\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{in}}$ ) by any Gaussian surface inside the conductor must also be zero. Therefore, any excess charge resides entirely on the outer surface.

Therefore, assertion A is true.

Inside a charged capacitor, there is a uniform electric field between the plates.

If free charge carriers (like electrons or ions) are placed in this region, they will experience an electric force ( $\mathrm{F}=\mathrm{qE}$ ). This force causes the charges to accelerate or drift toward the plate of opposite polarity.

Therefore, reason R is true.

While both statements are scientifically true, reason R describes the behaviour of charges in an external field between two conductors (the plates). It does not explain why the net charge inside a solid conductor is zero (which is due to mutual repulsion and the resulting zero internal field).

So, both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A .

Thus, the correct option is (B).

subject: physics
question_text:
A solenoid has a core made of material with relative permeability 400. The magnetic field produced in the interior of solenoid is 1.0 T. The magnetic intensity in SI units is $$\alpha \times 10^5$$. The value of $$\alpha$$ is ______.

(Free space permeability $$\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$$ SI units.)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The magnetic flux density, magnetic field strength and permeability are related by
$$B = \mu\,H = \mu_{0}\,\mu_{r}\,H$$

Hence
$$H = \frac{B}{\mu_{0}\,\mu_{r}}$$

Given data:
$$B = 1.0\ \text{T},\qquad \mu_{r} = 400,\qquad \mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{H m}^{-1}$$

Substituting the values:
$$H = \frac{1.0}{\bigl(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\bigr)\,(400)}$$

Simplify the denominator:
$$4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 400 = 1600\pi \times 10^{-7} = 1.6\times10^{-4}\,\pi$$

Therefore
$$H = \frac{1}{1.6\times10^{-4}\,\pi}\ \text{A m}^{-1}$$

Working out the numerical factor:
$$\frac{1}{1.6\times10^{-4}} = \frac{1}{1.6}\times10^{4} = 0.625\times10^{4} = 6.25\times10^{3}$$

Hence
$$H = \frac{6.25\times10^{3}}{\pi}\ \text{A m}^{-1}$$

Express this in the form $$H = \alpha \times 10^{5}\ \text{A m}^{-1}$$:
$$\frac{6.25\times10^{3}}{\pi} = \frac{0.0625\times10^{5}}{\pi}$$

Thus
$$\alpha = \frac{0.0625}{\pi} = \frac{1}{16\pi}$$

Therefore, the correct choice is:
Option B which is: $$\frac{1}{16\pi}$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The relative permeability of the core is $\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=400$.

The magnetic field applied is, $\mathrm{B}=1.0 \mathrm{~T}$.

The permeability of free space is $\mu_0=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~T} \cdot \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{A}$.

The magnetic induction $B$ in a material is related to the magnetic intensity $H$ by the total permeability of the medium ( $\mu$ ) :

$$ \mathrm{B}=\mu \mathrm{H} \ldots \text { (i) } $$

The total permeability $\mu$ is the product of the permeability of free space and the relative permeability of the material :

$$ \mu=\mu_0 \mu_r $$

Substituting this into the first equation :

$$ \mathrm{B}=\mu_0 \mu_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$$$ H=\frac{B}{\mu_0 \mu_r} $$

Substituting the given values,

$$ H=\frac{1.0}{\left(4 \pi \times 10^{-7}\right) \times 400} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $H=\frac{1}{1600 \pi \times 10^{-7}}$

$$\Rightarrow $$$$ H=\frac{1}{16 \pi} \times 10^5=a \times 10^5 \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{1}{16 \pi} $$

Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is $\frac{1}{16 \pi}$.

Thus, the correct option is (B).

subject: physics
question_text: A magnetic field vector in an electromagnetic wave is represented by $$\vec{B} = B_0\sin\left(2\pi\nu t - \frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}\right)\hat{j}$$. Its associated electric field vector is ______.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The given magnetic field of the electromagnetic (EM) wave is
$$\vec{B}=B_0\sin\!\left(2\pi\nu t-\frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}\right)\,\hat{j}$$

Step 1 — Identify the direction of propagation.
For a plane EM wave, the phase $$\left(2\pi\nu t-\frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}\right)$$ has the form $$\omega t-kx$$, which corresponds to a wave travelling along the $$+x$$-axis. Hence, the propagation vector $$\vec{k}$$ is along $$+\hat{i}$$.

Step 2 — Use the orthogonality of $$\vec{E},\;\vec{B}$$ and $$\vec{k}$$.
In a uniform EM wave, $$\vec{E}\perp\vec{B}\perp\vec{k}$$ and
$$\vec{E}\times\vec{B} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\,\vec{S}$$ points in the propagation direction $$\vec{k}$$(i.e. $$+\hat{i}$$ here).

Step 3 — Determine the unit vector for $$\vec{E}$$.
We already have $$\vec{k}=+\hat{i}$$ and $$\vec{B}$$ along $$+\hat{j}$$. Let $$\vec{E}$$ be along $$\hat{n}$$. We need
$$\hat{n}\times\hat{j}=+\hat{i}$$.
Using the right-hand rule: $$(-\hat{k})\times\hat{j}=+\hat{i}$$. Therefore $$\hat{n}=-\hat{k}$$ and $$\vec{E}$$ must be along $$-\hat{k}$$.

Step 4 — Relate the magnitudes $$E_0$$ and $$B_0$$.
In free space, $$E_0 = cB_0$$ where $$c$$ is the speed of light. Using $$c=\nu\lambda$$, we get
$$E_0 = \nu\lambda\,B_0$$.

Step 5 — Write the complete electric field.
Keeping the same phase factor as $$\vec{B}$$, the electric field is
$$\vec{E}= -\nu\lambda B_0 \sin\!\left(2\pi\nu t-\frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}\right)\hat{k}$$.

Thus the correct option is:
Option A which is: $$-\nu\lambda B_0 \sin\!\left(2\pi\nu t-\frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}\right)\hat{k}$$.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The argument of the sine function is $\left(2 \pi v t-\frac{2 \pi x}{\lambda}\right)$. This indicates the wave is propagating along the positive x -axis.

Let the unit vector for the direction of propagation be $\hat{\mathrm{n}}=\hat{\mathrm{i}}$.

In an electromagnetic wave, the electric field vector $(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}})$, the magnetic field vector $(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}})$, and the direction of propagation ( $\widehat{\mathrm{n}}$ ) are mutually perpendicular. Their relationship is given by:

$$ \widehat{\mathrm{E}}=\widehat{\mathrm{B}} \times \widehat{\mathrm{n}} $$

It is given that $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$ is along $\hat{\mathrm{j}}$ :

$$ \widehat{\mathrm{E}}=\hat{\jmath} \times \hat{\imath}=-\hat{\mathrm{k}} $$

The magnitude of the electric field and magnetic field in a vacuum are related by the speed of light (c):

$$ \mathrm{E}_0=\mathrm{cB}_0 $$

The speed of light is the product of frequency and wavelength: $\mathrm{c}=\nu \lambda$.

$$ \mathrm{E}_0=v \lambda \mathrm{~B}_0 $$

The electric field must have the same phase as the magnetic field. So, the electric field component is,

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=\mathrm{E}_0 \sin \left(2 \pi v \mathrm{t}-\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{x}}{\lambda}\right)(-\widehat{\mathrm{k}}) $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=-v \lambda \mathrm{~B}_0 \sin \left(2 \pi v \mathrm{t}-\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{x}}{\lambda}\right) \hat{\mathrm{k}} $$

Therefore, the associated electric field vector is $-v \lambda \mathrm{~B}_0 \sin \left(2 \pi v \mathrm{t}-\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{x}}{\lambda}\right) \hat{\mathrm{k}}$.

Thus, the correct option is (A).

subject: physics
question_text: A convex lens is made from glass material having refractive index of 1.4 with same radius of curvature on both sides. The ratio of its focal length and radius of curvature is ______.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The focal length of a thin lens kept in air is obtained from the Lens-Maker’s formula

$$\frac{1}{f}=(n-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{R_2}\right)$$

where
 • $$n$$ is the refractive index of the lens material with respect to air,
 • $$R_1$$ is the radius of curvature of the first surface (sign taken according to the Cartesian convention),
 • $$R_2$$ is the radius of curvature of the second surface.

The lens is given as a symmetric bi-convex lens, so the magnitudes of the radii are equal: $$|R_1| = |R_2| = R$$.

For light traveling from left to right:
 • The centre of curvature of the first surface lies to the right of that surface, hence $$R_1 = +R$$.
 • The centre of curvature of the second surface lies to the left of that surface, hence $$R_2 = -R$$.

Substituting these signs:

$$\frac{1}{f}=(n-1)\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{-R}\right)=(n-1)\left(\frac{1}{R}+\frac{1}{R}\right)=2(n-1)\frac{1}{R}$$

Rearranging for $$f$$:

$$f=\frac{R}{2(n-1)}$$

The given refractive index is $$n = 1.4$$, so $$n-1 = 0.4$$.

Therefore:

$$f=\frac{R}{2\times 0.4}=\frac{R}{0.8}=1.25\,R$$

Hence

$$\frac{f}{R}=1.25$$

Option D which is: $$1.25$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
For a thin lens with two curved surfaces, the focal length ( $f$ ) is related to the refractive index ( $n$ ) and the radii of curvature $\left(\mathrm{R}_1\right.$ and $\left.\mathrm{R}_2\right)$ by Lens Makers' formula,

$$ \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=(\mathrm{n}-1)\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right) $$

The refractive index of the material, $\mathrm{n}=1.4$.

The lens is convex with the same radius of curvature on both sides (R).

According to the Cartesian sign convention:

The first surface is convex towards the incident light, so $\mathrm{R}_1=+\mathrm{R}$.

The second surface is concave towards the incident light, so $R_2=-R$.

Substituting the values into the formula :

$$ \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=(1.4-1)\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}-\frac{1}{-\mathrm{R}}\right) $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=(0.4)\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\right)$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=0.4 \times \frac{2}{\mathrm{R}}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{f}=\frac{0.8}{R}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{f}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{0.8}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{\mathrm{f}}{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{1}{0.8}=1.25 $$

Therefore, the ratio of its focal length and radius of curvature is 1.25 .

Thus, the correct option is (D).

subject: physics
question_text: An unpolarized light of certain intensity passes through a combination of two polarizers whose transmission axes are at 30° and 90°, respectively, with respect to the horizontal axis. A third polarizer with its transmission axis at 60° with the horizontal axis is placed between the two existing polarizers. The ratio of the output intensities with and without the third polarizer is ______.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Let the intensity of the incident unpolarised light be $$I_0$$. When unpolarised light passes through a polariser, its intensity is reduced to half.

Case 1: Only the original two polarisers (axes at $$30^{\circ}$$ and $$90^{\circ}$$)
After the first polariser (axis $$30^{\circ}$$):
$$I_1 = \frac{I_0}{2}$$

The second polariser’s axis is at $$90^{\circ}$$, i.e. it is at an angle $$\theta = 90^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$$ to the first axis.
By Malus’ law, transmitted intensity is
$$I_{\text{without}} = I_1 \cos^{2} \theta = \frac{I_0}{2}\cos^{2}60^{\circ} = \frac{I_0}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{I_0}{8}$$

Case 2: A third polariser (axis $$60^{\circ}$$) inserted between the first two
Order of axes: $$30^{\circ} \rightarrow 60^{\circ} \rightarrow 90^{\circ}$$.

Step-1 First polariser (axis $$30^{\circ}$$):
$$I_1 = \frac{I_0}{2}$$

Step-2 Second polariser (axis $$60^{\circ}$$) is at $$30^{\circ}$$ to the first.
$$I_2 = I_1 \cos^{2}30^{\circ} = \frac{I_0}{2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{I_0}{2}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) = \frac{3I_0}{8}$$

Step-3 Third polariser (axis $$90^{\circ}$$) is at $$30^{\circ}$$ to the second.
$$I_{\text{with}} = I_2 \cos^{2}30^{\circ} = \frac{3I_0}{8}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{3I_0}{8}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) = \frac{9I_0}{32}$$

Required ratio
$$\frac{I_{\text{with}}}{I_{\text{without}}} = \frac{\dfrac{9I_0}{32}}{\dfrac{I_0}{8}} = \frac{9}{32}\times\frac{8}{1} = \frac{9}{4}$$

Hence, the intensity becomes $$\dfrac{9}{4}$$ times larger when the third polariser at $$60^{\circ}$$ is inserted.

Option C which is: $$\frac{9}{4}$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
When polarized light of intensity $\mathrm{I}_{\text {in }}$ passes through a polarizer, the intensity of the transmitted light $\left(\mathrm{I}_{\text {out }}\right)$ is given by Malus's Law

$$ I_{\text {out }}=I_{\text {in }} \cos ^2 \theta $$

Where $\theta$ is the angle between the polarization direction of the incident light and the transmission axis of the polarizer.

The initial intensity of unpolarised light $=\mathrm{I}_0$.

After the first polarizer (at $30^{\circ}$ ), the light becomes polarized with intensity $\mathrm{I}_1=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I}_0$.

This light then hits the second polarizer (at $90^{\circ}$ ). The angle between them is $\theta=90^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$.

So, the final intensity without third polarizer is,

$$ I_{\text {withoud }}=I_2=I_1 \cos ^2 60^{\circ}=\left(\frac{1}{2} I_0\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2} I_0 \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{I_0}{8} $$

The intensity after the first polarizer (at $30^{\circ}$ ) is $\mathrm{I}_1=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I}_0$.

This light hits the middle polarizer (at $60^{\circ}$ ). The angle is $\theta_{12}=60^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=30^{\circ}$.

So, intensity after middle polarizer $\left(\mathrm{I}_3\right)$ :

$$ I_3=I_1 \cos ^2 30^{\circ}=\left(\frac{1}{2} I_0\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2} I_0 \times \frac{3}{4}=\frac{3 I_0}{8} $$

This light hits the final polarizer (at $90^{\circ}$ ). The angle is $\theta_{23}=90^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=30^{\circ}$.

So, final intensity after the final polarizer is

$$ \mathrm{I}_{\text {with }}=\mathrm{I}_3 \cos ^2 30^{\circ}=\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{I}_0}{8}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2=\frac{3 \mathrm{I}_0}{8} \times \frac{3}{4}=\frac{9 \mathrm{I}_0}{32} $$

So, the ratio of the output intensities with and without the third polarizer is,

$$ \frac{\mathrm{I}_{\text {with }}}{\mathrm{I}_{\text {without }}}=\frac{\left(\frac{9 \mathrm{I}_0}{32}\right)}{\left(\frac{\mathrm{I}_0}{8}\right)}=\frac{9}{4} $$

Therefore, the ratio of the output intensities with and without the third polarizer is $9 / 4$.

Thus, the correct option is (C).

subject: physics
question_text:
In Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, only a few alpha particles rebound back because

A. The size of gold nucleus is very small as compared to the size of gold atom.

B. Alpha particle and gold nucleus have equal charge.

C. The impact parameter is minimum for a few alpha particles.

D. A few alpha particles have very high kinetic energy.

E. Only a few alpha particles undergo head-on collision with the nuclei.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The question asks why, in Rutherford’s gold-foil experiment, only a very small fraction of incident $$\alpha$$-particles are scattered backward (rebound through angles $$\gt 90^{\circ}$$).
To answer, recall two key ideas of Rutherford scattering:

1. The nuclear size is extremely small compared with the atomic size.
2. Large deflection (up to $$180^{\circ}$$) occurs only when the $$\alpha$$-particle passes very close to the nucleus, i.e. the impact parameter $$b$$ is extremely small. Such trajectories are often called “head-on” or “near head-on” collisions.

Using these ideas, examine each statement:

Statement A: “The gold nucleus is very small compared to the atom.”
Because the nucleus occupies only about $$10^{-15}\text{ m}$$ while the atom is about $$10^{-10}\text{ m}$$, the geometrical area that can give large deflection is tiny. Hence very few $$\alpha$$-particles come close enough to rebound. Statement A is correct.

Statement B: “$$\alpha$$-particle and gold nucleus have equal charge.”
The charges are $$+2e$$ for an $$\alpha$$-particle and $$+79e$$ for a gold nucleus; they are not equal. Therefore Statement B is wrong.

Statement C: “Impact parameter is minimum for very few particles.”
The distribution of $$\alpha$$-particles over the foil is uniform, so only a minute fraction possess a sufficiently small impact parameter $$b$$ ($$b \approx 0$$) required for large-angle scattering. Hence Statement C is correct.

Statement D: “Very few $$\alpha$$-particles have very high kinetic energy.”
All $$\alpha$$-particles in Rutherford’s beam are emitted from the same radioactive source and have nearly the same kinetic energy. The fraction with “very high” energy is not the reason for rare back-scattering. Statement D is wrong.

Statement E: “Only few $$\alpha$$-particles undergo head-on collision.”
A head-on collision corresponds to $$b \approx 0$$ and produces a $$180^{\circ}$$ reversal. Since $$b \approx 0$$ events are rare, only a few $$\alpha$$-particles rebound. Statement E is correct.

Thus the correct set of reasons is A, C, and E.

Therefore, the correct option is
Option D which is: A, C, E Only.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
In the experiment, alpha particles (positively charged helium nuclei) are fired at a thin gold foil. Rutherford observed that most particles passed straight through, but a tiny fraction (about 1 in 8000 ) reflected back at angles greater than $90^{\circ}$.

Statement A: Rutherford concluded that the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in an extremely small region called the nucleus. Since the nucleus is tiny compared to the total volume of the atom, the probability of an alpha particle hitting it or coming close enough to be repelled backward is very low.

Hence, statement A is true.

Statement B: Alpha particles have a charge of +2 e , while a gold nucleus has a charge of +79 e . They do not have equal charges. Hence, statement B is false.

Statement C: The impact parameter (b) is the perpendicular distance of the initial velocity vector of the alpha particle from the centre of the nucleus.

A rebound or large-angle scattering occurs when the impact parameter is very small (close to zero), meaning the particle is heading almost directly toward the nucleus. Only a few particles have such a small impact parameter. Hence, the statement C is true.

Statement D: The kinetic energy of the incident alpha particles is generally uniform in the beam; high kinetic energy would actually make it easier to penetrate closer to the nucleus rather than causing the few rebounds mentioned. Hence, the statement D is false.

Statement E: A head-on collision occurs when the particle moves directly toward the centre of the nucleus $(\mathrm{b}=0)$. Because the nucleus is so small, only a very small number of particles are aligned for such a collision. Hence, the statement E is true.

Therefore, statements A, C, and E are the correct reasons for the observed phenomenon.

Thus, the correct option is (D).

subject: physics
question_text: The de Broglie wavelength associated with an electron accelerated through a potential difference V is $$\lambda_e$$ and the de Broglie wavelength associated with a proton accelerated through the same potential difference is $$\lambda_p$$. If their corresponding masses are $$m_e$$ and $$m_p$$, respectively, then the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths $$\left(\frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p}\right)$$ is ______.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The de Broglie wavelength of any particle is given by $$\lambda=\frac{h}{p}$$, where $$h$$ is Planck’s constant and $$p$$ is the linear momentum of the particle.

When a charged particle of charge magnitude $$e$$ is accelerated from rest through a potential difference $$V$$, the gain in kinetic energy is $$eV$$. Hence for a particle of mass $$m$$:

$$\text{K.E.}=eV=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}\; \Longrightarrow\; p=\sqrt{2meV}$$

Substituting this in the de Broglie formula:

$$\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}$$ $$-(1)$$

Both the electron (mass $$m_e$$) and the proton (mass $$m_p$$) are accelerated through the same potential difference $$V$$, so the factor $$\sqrt{2eV}$$ is common. Writing their wavelengths from $$(1)$$:

$$\lambda_e=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_e eV}}, \qquad \lambda_p=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_p eV}}$$

Taking the ratio:

$$\frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p} =\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_e eV}}\;\Big/\;\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_p eV}} =\frac{1}{\sqrt{m_e}}\times\sqrt{m_p} =\sqrt{\frac{m_p}{m_e}}$$

Therefore $$\frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p}=\sqrt{\frac{m_p}{m_e}}$$.

Option A which is: $$\sqrt{\frac{m_p}{m_e}}$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
According to de Broglie's hypothesis, the wavelength associated with a particle of momentum p is:

$$ \lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{p}} $$

Where h is Planck's constant.

Kinetic energy is given by $\mathrm{K}=\frac{1}{2 \mathrm{mv}^2}$.

In terms of linear momentum, the kinetic energy can be written as

$$ K=\frac{m^2 v^2}{2 m}=\frac{p^2}{2 m} $$

Thus, momentum $\mathrm{p}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mK}}$.

When a particle of charge q is accelerated through a potential difference V , the work done on it becomes its kinetic energy:

$$ \mathrm{K}=\mathrm{qV} $$

Substituting this into the momentum equation:

$$ \mathrm{p}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mqV}} $$

So, the de-Broglie's wavelength is $\lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mqV}}}$

The charge on electron is $\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{e}}=\mathrm{e}$, so the wavelength for an electron is $\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{eV}}}$

The charge on proton is $\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{e}$, so the wavelength for an proton is $\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{p}} \mathrm{eV}}}$

Taking the ratio $\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}}$ :

$$ \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}}=\frac{\mathrm{h} / \sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{eV}}}{\mathrm{~h} / \sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{p}} \mathrm{eV}}}=\frac{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{p}} \mathrm{eV}}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{eV}}} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{e}}}} $$

Therefore, the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths is $\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{e}}}}$.

Thus, the correct option is (A).

subject: physics
question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R

Assertion A: A diode under reverse-biased condition provides very small current which is nearly independent of voltage until a critical limit at which the current increases drastically.

Reason R: Below the critical voltage limit, only majority charge carriers flow which increases drastically above critical voltage.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
In a $$p$$-$$n$$ junction diode the biasing conditions decide the direction and magnitude of current.
Let the applied voltage be $$V$$ with the convention that forward bias is positive and reverse bias is negative.

Behaviour under reverse bias
  • When the junction is reverse-biased, the depletion region widens and the majority carriers are repelled away from the junction.
  • The only carriers that are able to cross the junction are the thermally generated minority carriers (electrons in the $$p$$-region and holes in the $$n$$-region).
  • Their concentration is fixed by temperature, not by the magnitude of the reverse voltage (as long as the electric field is below the breakdown limit).
  • Hence the reverse current remains almost constant and is called the reverse saturation current $$I_S$$.

When the reverse voltage magnitude becomes large enough, the electric field in the depletion region exceeds a critical value. Avalanche multiplication (or Zener tunnelling, depending on doping) starts, causing a sudden, very large increase in reverse current. This point is called the breakdown voltage $$V_{BR}$$.

Verification of Assertion (A)
The statement in (A) says: “A reverse-biased diode gives a small current independent of voltage until a critical limit is reached.”
This is exactly the description of the constant reverse saturation current up to the breakdown voltage. Therefore Assertion (A) is true.

Verification of Reason (R)
Reason (R) states: “Below the critical voltage, only majority carriers flow.”
This is incorrect because, under reverse bias, majority carriers are blocked by the widened potential barrier. The small reverse current is due to minority carriers, not majority carriers. Hence the Reason (R) is false.

Relationship between A and R
Since (A) is true and (R) is false, (R) cannot be the correct explanation of (A).

Therefore, the correct choice is:
Option C which is: A is true but R is false.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
In reverse bias, the positive terminal of the battery is connected to the n-side and the negative terminal to the p-side. This widens the depletion layer and increases the potential barrier.

Only a very small current, known as the reverse saturation current, flows.

This current is caused by the drift of minority charge carriers (electrons in p-type and holes in n-type) across the junction.

Because the number of minority carriers is small and depends mainly on temperature, the current remains nearly constant (independent of voltage) until a high enough voltage, called the Zener or Breakdown voltage, is reached.

At this critical limit, the current increases drastically due to junction breakdown. Therefore, Assertion A is true.

So, the current flowing below the breakdown voltage is due to minority charge carriers, not majority carriers.

Majority carriers are pushed away from the junction in reverse bias, which is why they do not contribute to the current. Therefore, the statement that "only majority charge carriers flow" is incorrect in the reverse bias. Therefore, Reason R is false.

Thus, assertion A is true, but reason R is false.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

subject: physics
question_text: A diode has Zener voltage of 10 V and maximum power dissipation of 0.5 W, then the minimum resistance to be used in series with this diode for safety when it is connected to a 25 V power supply is ______ $$\Omega$$.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The Zener diode will operate in its breakdown (regulating) region when the voltage across it is $$V_Z = 10\text{ V}$$.

Its maximum power dissipation is $$P_{\text{max}} = 0.5\text{ W}$$.
Using the power formula $$P = VI$$, the maximum permissible current through the Zener is

$$I_{\text{Z(max)}} = \frac{P_{\text{max}}}{V_Z} = \frac{0.5\text{ W}}{10\text{ V}} = 0.05\text{ A} = 50\text{ mA}.$$

The supply voltage is $$V_S = 25\text{ V}$$. A series resistor $$R_S$$ is placed so that, at the worst case (no external load, all current through the Zener), the current does not exceed $$I_{\text{Z(max)}}$$.

Applying Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law:

$$V_S = I_{\text{Z}}\,R_S + V_Z.$$

At the limiting condition, $$I_{\text{Z}} = I_{\text{Z(max)}}$$. Hence

$$R_S = \frac{V_S - V_Z}{I_{\text{Z(max)}}} = \frac{25\text{ V} - 10\text{ V}}{0.05\text{ A}} = \frac{15\text{ V}}{0.05\text{ A}} = 300\ \Omega.$$

Therefore, the minimum series resistance required is 300 Ω.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Power $(\mathrm{P})$ dissipated in a Zener diode is the product of the Zener voltage $\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{z}}\right)$ and the current through it $\left(\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{z}}\right)$ :

$$ \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{z}} \times \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{z}} $$

For maximum current (I_max) :

$$ I_{\max }=\frac{P_{\max }}{V_Z} $$

Substituting the given values ( $\mathrm{P}_{\max }=0.5 \mathrm{~W}, \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{z}}=10 \mathrm{~V}$ ):

$$ I_{\max }=\frac{0.5}{10}=0.05 \mathrm{~A} \text { or } 50 \mathrm{~mA} $$

The diode is connected to a power supply ( $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}}=25 \mathrm{~V}$ ) in series with a resistor (R). According to Kirchhoff's Voltage Law :

$$ V_s=V_R+V_z $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ V_R=V_s-V_z $$

Substituting the values:

$$ \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{R}}=25-10=15 \mathrm{~V} $$

To keep the diode safe, the current in the circuit should not exceed $\mathrm{I}_{\max }$.

From Ohm's Law ( $\mathrm{V}=\mathrm{IR}$ ) :

$$ \mathrm{R}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{R}}}{\mathrm{I}} $$

To find the minimum resistance that limits the current to exactly $\mathrm{I}_{\max }$ :

$$ \mathrm{R}_{\min }=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{R}}}{\mathrm{I}_{\max }} $$

Substituting the values :

$$ \mathrm{R}_{\min }=\frac{15}{0.05} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{R}_{\min }=\frac{1500}{5}=300 \Omega $$

Therefore, the minimum resistance to be used in series is $300 \Omega$.

Hence, the correct answer is 300 .

subject: physics
question_text:
A gun mounted on the ground fires bullets in all directions with same speed. The farthest distance the bullets could reach is 6.4 m. The speed of the bullets from the gun is ______ m/s.

(take $$g = 10$$ m/s$$^2$$)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
For a projectile fired with initial speed $$u$$ at an angle $$\theta$$ to the horizontal, the horizontal range is given by
$$R = \frac{u^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g}$$.

The range becomes maximum when $$\sin 2\theta = 1$$, i.e. when $$2\theta = 90^{\circ}$$ or $$\theta = 45^{\circ}$$. Hence the maximum range is
$$R_{\max} = \frac{u^{2}}{g}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,-(1)$$

Given $$R_{\max} = 6.4\text{ m}$$ and $$g = 10\text{ m/s}^{2}$$. Substituting these values in $$(1)$$:
$$6.4 = \frac{u^{2}}{10}$$

$$u^{2} = 6.4 \times 10 = 64$$

$$u = \sqrt{64} = 8 \text{ m/s}$$

Therefore, the speed of the bullets is 8 m/s.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
A bullet fired with an initial velocity $u$ at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. On resolving the initial velocity of bullet.

Horizontal component: $\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{u} \cos \theta$

Vertical component: $\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{u} \sin \theta$

The time of flight $(T)$ is the time taken for the bullet to return to the ground $(y=0)$.

Using the equation $\mathrm{y}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{y}} \mathrm{t}-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{gt}^2$ :

$$ 0=(\mathrm{u} \sin \theta) \mathrm{T}-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{gT}^2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~T}=\frac{2 \mathrm{u} \sin \theta}{\mathrm{~g}} $$

The horizontal range $(\mathrm{R})$ is the distance covered during this time :

$$ \mathrm{R}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}} \times \mathrm{T}=(\mathrm{u} \cos \theta)\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{u} \sin \theta}{\mathrm{~g}}\right) $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{R}=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin (2 \theta)}{\mathrm{g}}$

The range is maximum when $\sin (2 \theta)$ is maximum. The maximum value of the sine function is 1 (which occurs when $2 \theta=90^{\circ} \Rightarrow \theta=45^{\circ}$ ).

So, the maximum horizontal range is

$$ \mathrm{R}_{\max }=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2}{\mathrm{~g}} $$

The maximum horizontal range is given as 6.4 m

$$ 6.4=\frac{u^2}{10} \Rightarrow u^2=64 \Rightarrow u=8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$

Therefore, the speed of the bullets from the gun is $8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

Hence, the correct answer is 8 .

subject: physics
question_text:
Two identical small bar magnets each of dipole moment $$3\sqrt{5}$$ J/T are placed at a center to center separation of 10 cm, with their axes perpendicular to each other as shown in figure. The value of magnetic field at the point P midway between the magnets is $$\alpha \times 10^{-3}$$ T. The value of $$\alpha$$ is ______

($$\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$$ Tm/A)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The centres of the two identical magnets are $$10 \text{ cm}=0.10 \text{ m}$$ apart, so the midpoint $$P$$ is at a distance $$r=\dfrac{0.10}{2}=0.05 \text{ m}$$ from each magnet.

Choose the geometry so that the axis of magnet 1 lies along the line joining the two centres, while the axis of magnet 2 is perpendicular to that line (the axes are given to be perpendicular).
• Therefore, point $$P$$ is on the axial line of magnet 1.
• The same point $$P$$ is on the equatorial line of magnet 2.
